prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item also shows your previous context and question. Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key ed545d48e7a8
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to train the model to give verbalized probabilities, given that cross-entropy against the ground-truth answer is only usable for the indirect logit.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2022-06-01, on "Paper: Teaching GPT3 to express uncertainty in words" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/vbfAwZqKs84agyGWC/paper-teaching-gpt3-to-express-uncertainty-in-words?commentId=C8gJmnbiiBJxaoN7R PARENT (not his words): I was surprised by how the fine-tuning was done for the verbalized confidence. My initial expectation was that it would make the loss be based on like, some scoring rule based on the probability expressed and the right answer. Though, come to think of it, I guess seeing as it would be assigning logits values to different expressions of probabilities, it would have to... what, take the weighted average of the scores it would get if it gave the different probabilities? And, I suppose that if many training steps were done on the same question/answer pairs, then the confidences might just get pushed towards 0% or 100%? Ah, but for the indirect logit it was trained using the "is it right or wrong" with the cross-entropy loss thing. Ok, cool. HIS COMMENT: The indirect logit is trained with cross-entropy based on the groundtruth correct answer.
Previous context: A team is fine-tuning a language model to state its confidence in its own answers, either as a verbalized probability or as a probability read from the logit of an extra token. For the logit version, standard cross-entropy against whether the answer is correct can be used. For a verbalized probability, no single ground-truth correct probability exists for each question, so the same loss does not directly apply.
Previous question: How should the team construct the training signal for the model to give well-calibrated verbalized probabilities?

=== key 5494480f190e
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: It is unknown whether the benefit of paraphrased training data comes from raw diversity or from a few specific paraphrases.
Write-up text before the decision: Comment by Owain_Evans, 2023-09-06, on "Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mLfPHv4QjmeQrsSva/paper-on-measuring-situational-awareness-in-llms?commentId=rWGg4X3okzKwaPz9D PARENT (not his words): Cool paper! I'd be keen to see more examples of the paraphrases, if you're able to share. To get a sense of the kind of data that lets the model generalize out of context. (E.g. if it'd be easy to take all 300 paraphrases of some statement (ideally where performance improved) and paste in a google doc and share. Or lmk if this is on github somewhere.) I'd also be interested in experiments to determine whether the benefit from paraphrases is mostly fueled by the raw diversity, or if it's because examples with certain specific features help a bunch, and those occasionally appear among the paraphrases. Curious if you have a prediction about that or if you already ran some experiments that shed some light on this. (I could have missed it even if it was in the paper.) HIS COMMENT: We didn't investigate the specific question of whether it's raw diversity or specific features. In the Grosse et al [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03296) on influence functions, they find that "high influence scores are relatively rare and they cover a large portion of the total influence".
Previous context: A research team found that fine-tuning on many paraphrases of a fact improves a model's out-of-context generalization. A reader asks whether the benefit comes from raw diversity across many paraphrases or from a few paraphrases with particular helpful features. The team did not run an experiment to separate these. Related work on influence functions found that high influence scores are rare but account for a large share of the total influence.
Previous question: How strongly should the team state a claim about why paraphrases help, given that they did not test diversity against specific features?
